newsitem.title: UK: UK's first two offshore wind farms get green light.
newsitem.headline: UK's first two offshore wind farms get green light.

text.p: Britain gave the go-ahead on Monday for development of the country's first two offshore wind farms, the Department of Trade and Industry said in a statement.

Junior energy minister Richard Page awarded Windmaster Developments Ltd and Border Wind Ltd contracts to build wind power generation projects off the eastern and north-eastern coast of England respectively.
Border Wind technical director Bill Grainger said they hoped to get the project up and running by the summer of 1998. Windmaster Developments were not available for comment.
"We're trailblazing it for them and the rest of the industry," Grainger said. "Offshore wind could be quite big in five or 10 years time because of the objections to land-based sites."
Border Wind plan a demonstration project using two turbines capable of producing 850 kilo watts, the amount of electricity needed to power 1,000 average houses, he said.

The turbines, which will be sunk into the North Sea bed one kilometre from the shore in water between five and 10 metres deep, will have two 45 metre diameter wings from the top of a 50 metre high stand.
Similar projects have been set up in lakes in Denmark and Holland but Border Wind managing director David Still said this project would be the first of its kind in such exposed waters.
Grainger said the demonstration project would use turbines built by Windmaster Developments and would serve as a dry run for their large scale 40 turbine windfarm project.

The awards are among 195 contracts given under the government's fourth Non-fossil Fuel Obligation Order (NFFO-4) which aims to create 843 mega watts generating capacity via alternative energy sources.

Other renewable energy projects given approval were 70 using landfill gas, 16 from waste, 65 from wind -(including the offshore projects), 31 from hydro, six from farm waste, and seven from energy crops.
Page said the 195 approved projects would need to apply for planning permission in the normal way before getting off the ground.
